video_title: Dick Costolo (Former Twitter CEO) on Elon, AI, and What's Next
gist: Former Twitter CEO Dick Costolo, now co-founder of early-growth VC firm 01 Advisors, lays out his thesis for investing in the AI 'enablement layer' (inference, data, security infrastructure) and the coming physical-AI/robotics wave, while warning that seed-stage valuations (not growth-stage) are the real bubble risk. He and host Dan Nathan dissect Stripe's roughly $7B acquisition of OpenRouter, diverging expectations for the SpaceX/Anthropic/OpenAI IPOs, and draw lessons from Twitter, Google, and Clubhouse on why platform virality can't be engineered or copied.

insights.claim: 01 Advisors (co-founded by Dick Costolo and Adam Bain in 2018) invests specifically at the early-growth stage (roughly Series B), after a startup has product-market fit but before it has learned to scale go-to-market, operating leverage, and management -- a stage they say was underserved after mentor/coach Bill Campbell's death left no equivalent operator-investor for that phase.
insights.speaker: Dick Costolo
insights.so_what: Signals a durable structural gap in the VC stack (post-PMF, pre-scale) that 01 Advisors is deliberately positioned to fill -- useful for mapping where competitive/capital pressure is lighter.
insights.quote: You got to go from building a product to scaling a company.

insights.claim: 01 Advisors avoids AI foundation models and end-user apps, instead concentrating on the 'enablement layer' that sits above the models and services every model and application -- citing five investments in inference company Base10, a data company called Micro1 (a Mercor competitor), and an AI security company that was later acquired by Palo Alto Networks.
insights.speaker: Dick Costolo
insights.so_what: A concrete, repeatable picks-and-shovels framework for AI infrastructure exposure that avoids model-layer commoditization risk and app-layer churn.
insights.quote: We love these companies that sit above the models and can service a a all the models and b all the applications and other services that sit on top of those.

insights.claim: Unlike prior tech booms (e.g., the dot-com-era 'Silicon Alley' hype that never rivaled Silicon Valley), this AI cycle has produced genuinely strong hubs outside the Bay Area -- 01 Advisors has invested in two London AI companies, Adia (an AI-native CRM platform) and Fractile (an inference-chip company), plus multiple New York companies including Crosby Legal, Long Lake, and Finch.
insights.speaker: Dick Costolo
insights.so_what: Investors sourcing AI deal flow should widen geographic scope beyond Silicon Valley this cycle rather than assume prior 'Silicon Alley'-style hype patterns will repeat (i.e., fizzle out).
insights.quote: there's a New York is Silicon Alley.

insights.claim: As a roughly 12-person firm competing against giants like Thrive Capital and Andreessen Horowitz, 01 Advisors deliberately narrows focus to the AI enablement layer and an emerging robotics/physical-AI enablement thesis rather than trying to cover the entire market.
insights.speaker: Dick Costolo
insights.so_what: Illustrates a disciplined small-fund strategy of thematic concentration over generalist coverage as a way to compete against mega-funds in a high-velocity market.

themes.theme: Growth valuations vs. seed-stage bubble risk

insights.claim: Costolo is less worried about high Series B/growth valuations because current AI-era revenue growth rates dwarf historical benchmarks like Twitter's own 0-to-$2.5B run (second only to Facebook, on par with Amazon) -- some companies are now going from $0 to $150M in a year, meaning a seemingly rich price-to-revenue multiple can look cheap 12 months later.
insights.speaker: Dick Costolo
insights.so_what: Argues against using historical SaaS/social growth benchmarks to flag AI growth-stage rounds as overpriced; revenue trajectory, not static multiples, should drive the valuation read.
insights.quote: The revenue growth is like this company went from zero to 150 in a year and that company went from zero to 15 and then 15 to 500. It's crazy.

insights.claim: Costolo's bigger concern is seed-stage rounds where founders with just an idea and no product are raising hundreds of millions of dollars at multi-billion-dollar valuations, arguing very few 'three people in a garage' companies will ever become trillion-dollar businesses.
insights.speaker: Dick Costolo
insights.so_what: Flags seed/pre-product AI rounds -- not growth-stage AI rounds -- as the segment most likely to disappoint investors on a risk-adjusted basis.
insights.quote: There aren't going to be that many three people in a garage that go to a trillion dollar businesses.

insights.claim: Because AI-era companies are staying private for much longer, early-stage investors are compiling large unrealized markups (TVPI) without actual distributions (DPI), meaning paper returns may not convert into real, returned capital for years.
insights.speaker: Dick Costolo
insights.so_what: A durability-of-returns warning for LPs evaluating seed/early-A funds: high reported multiples can mask a real liquidity problem.
insights.quote: TVPI you know markups are not DPI as any as any LP will tell you.

insights.claim: The venture return profile has historically reversed: seed used to be where the biggest returns were made because entry prices were lowest, but seed prices are now so high and competition so intense that it has become one of the harder stages to make money in.
insights.speaker: Dick Costolo
insights.so_what: Investors defaulting to a 'get in at seed' strategy should recognize that assumption no longer reliably holds in the current AI cycle.

themes.theme: Stripe's OpenRouter deal and AI infrastructure economics

insights.claim: Stripe is acquiring OpenRouter for roughly $7 billion, versus OpenRouter's last private valuation of about $1.3 billion in May 2026 -- Costolo frames it as 'Stripe 2.0,' i.e., Stripe building the payment/usage rails specifically for AI model routing and billing.
insights.speaker: host
insights.so_what: A large, fast markup on an AI-infrastructure deal signals how aggressively incumbents are paying up to own the 'rails' layer of the AI stack before competitors do.
insights.quote: Stripe is making a seven billion dollar you know um acquisition of Open Router

insights.claim: A leaked letter from Stripe co-founders John and Patrick Collison to their investors reportedly stated they believe 'the singularity' effectively happened on New Year's Day, underscoring how seriously major AI-infrastructure operators are treating recent capability jumps when making acquisition decisions.
insights.speaker: Dick Costolo
insights.so_what: A data point on how insiders building AI infrastructure privately calibrate the pace of AI progress -- relevant context for pricing AI-adjacent assets.
insights.quote: they believe the singularity um actually happened on New Year's Day.

insights.claim: Costolo believes competitive pressure from Ramp -- which has reportedly built its own in-house 'open router' equivalent and is ready to launch it -- likely added urgency and pushed Stripe to pay more for OpenRouter than it otherwise would have.
insights.speaker: Dick Costolo
insights.so_what: A reminder that AI-infrastructure M&A pricing is being driven partly by fear of a fast-follower competitor, not just standalone valuation logic.
insights.quote: RAMP has built their own open router basically and is ready to launch it if they haven't launched it already.

insights.claim: Hot AI startups like Cognition can decline acquisition offers because they can raise essentially unlimited capital in private markets and let founders sell secondary shares directly, removing the traditional pressure to exit via M&A.
insights.speaker: Dick Costolo
insights.so_what: Explains why strategic acquirers are having to pay premium prices (as with OpenRouter) to win over founders who otherwise have no financial need to sell.

insights.claim: Costolo expects three very different outcomes for the SpaceX, Anthropic, and OpenAI IPOs, despite all three being framed together as 'trillion-dollar' mega-listings.
insights.speaker: Dick Costolo
insights.so_what: Investors should not treat the three AI-adjacent mega-IPOs as a single homogeneous trade; execution and governance quality diverge sharply among them.
insights.quote: I think that actually there'll be three different IPOs even though it may seem very very similar.

insights.claim: Costolo expects retail investors and Elon Musk loyalists (including Cathie Wood) to support SpaceX stock regardless of whether specific promises materialize, citing Musk's 2024 claim of a million robotaxis on the road by end of 2025 versus roughly 63 actually operating in Austin, Texas -- arguing Musk's pattern of pivoting to 'the next story' (Mars, Optimus) has repeatedly insulated Tesla's stock from missed targets.
insights.speaker: Dick Costolo
insights.so_what: Suggests SpaceX's IPO pricing/performance may be driven more by narrative and fanbase conviction than by near-term delivery against stated milestones.
insights.quote: he said in 2024, by the end of 2025, there will be a million robo taxis on the road. I think there are 63 in Austin, Texas.

insights.claim: Costolo expects Anthropic to have a strong IPO because it has proven disciplined, focused enterprise go-to-market execution.
insights.speaker: Dick Costolo
insights.so_what: Positions Anthropic as the 'clean' execution story among the three AI-adjacent IPOs, a potential relative-value long versus OpenAI.
insights.quote: I think Anthropic will have a great IPO.

insights.claim: Costolo sees more IPO risk for OpenAI given a pattern of launching and then killing products (e.g., Sora), rapid executive churn (a CRO who lasted nine months, Greg Brockman departing and returning, Fidji Simo becoming president and then leaving), and CFO Sarah Friar having to publicly explain deals like the roughly $6B commitment to Nvidia that reads more like an understanding than a firm commitment; he expects OpenAI to target an IPO around 2027, likely after Anthropic's listing.
insights.speaker: Dick Costolo
insights.so_what: Flags governance/execution volatility (not AI demand) as OpenAI's key IPO risk factor -- worth monitoring executive turnover and vendor-commitment disclosures ahead of any listing.

insights.claim: Costolo argues that because Anthropic and OpenAI's most recent private valuations already sit well above where comparable public AI/hyperscaler stocks have traded (which have sold off roughly 25-30%), there is unlikely to ever be a public 'markdown' IPO for either company, since pricing below the last private round would risk puncturing broader AI valuation sentiment.
insights.speaker: Dick Costolo
insights.so_what: Implies IPO pricing for marquee AI names will be managed to avoid a down-round optics problem, which could mean IPO pricing is more about signaling than fair-value discovery.
insights.quote: if these were publicly traded companies right now, they'd easily be down 25 30%.

themes.theme: VC liquidity cycle and LP capital flows

insights.claim: Costolo expects the SpaceX, OpenAI, and Anthropic IPOs to act as major liquidity events that let LPs -- university endowments, pension funds, and similar institutions that have been sitting on paper markups with no distributions -- redeploy meaningfully more capital into venture funds over the next year.
insights.speaker: Dick Costolo
insights.so_what: A fresh wave of LP capital returning to venture next year is a leading indicator for further valuation inflation, especially at seed, worth tracking via fund closes and LP commitment data.

insights.claim: Costolo links the Trump administration's pressure on university research funding to endowments needing to devote more capital to research budgets, adding to institutional LPs' appetite for liquidity from existing private-market holdings.
insights.speaker: Dick Costolo
insights.so_what: Connects a policy/macro variable (federal research funding pressure) to venture-capital liquidity dynamics -- a less obvious causal chain investors may be underweighting.

insights.claim: More capital flowing back into venture from the anticipated 2026-2027 mega-IPO liquidity wave is expected to push seed valuations even higher due to increased competition for a limited pool of quality early-stage deals.
insights.speaker: Dick Costolo
insights.so_what: Reinforces the seed-stage-as-highest-risk thesis: incremental LP capital returning to venture is likely to exacerbate, not relieve, seed overpricing.
insights.quote: where there's tons more supply, they're going to be even higher seed valuations.

themes.theme: Platform lessons: Google, Twitter, and the social wars

insights.claim: Costolo argues Google, despite dominating via YouTube and Waymo, structurally cannot replicate a viral social network because its network lacks a virality mechanism -- its algorithm can serve content but cannot generate the organic spread that made products like early Twitter and Instagram take off.
insights.speaker: Dick Costolo
insights.so_what: Investors betting on Google entering social again should discount that scenario; the company's core distribution advantage doesn't transfer to social/viral products.
insights.quote: there's no ability in the Google network for verality. Yes, the algo will serve you.

insights.claim: Costolo says platform breakout success (Twitter, Instagram) comes down to being the right product at the right time with the right early crowd -- a dynamic that can't be manufactured or copied later, citing internal Twitter skepticism toward early Instagram ('there's already filters, Hipstamatic has filters') and his own failed attempt to acquire Instagram shortly before Facebook did.
insights.speaker: Dick Costolo
insights.so_what: A caution against assuming feature parity or capital alone can dislodge an incumbent network -- relevant when evaluating challengers trying to copy an established social product.

insights.claim: Costolo says live audio/video products structurally don't scale -- the same dynamic that sank Twitter's own live-streamed earnings calls on Periscope also doomed Clubhouse (which he says Andreessen Horowitz should have consulted him on before investing) and eventually Twitter's own Spaces feature.
insights.speaker: Dick Costolo
insights.so_what: A durable pattern-recognition heuristic for evaluating any new live-audio/live-video product pitch: live formats have repeatedly failed to scale as consumer products.
insights.quote: live is really really hard. It's really hard and it doesn't scale.

insights.claim: Costolo attributes recent traction at Threads and Bluesky not to superior product design but to a critical mass of users fed up with how Twitter/X has been run since Elon Musk's acquisition.
insights.speaker: Dick Costolo
insights.so_what: Suggests X's user-dissatisfaction is a direct tailwind for Meta's Threads and Bluesky -- a factor to weigh in assessing their growth durability versus organic product-market fit.
insights.quote: I think the reason threads and maybe blue sky are working a little bit now is because there were just enough of a critical mass of people who are fed up with the way Twitter was being run.

insights.claim: Costolo floated that Netflix should acquire Snap, arguing Snap has under-monetized, moveable video/clip distribution capability that neither Twitter/X nor Instagram offers, even though Snap's core teen demographic doesn't match Netflix's paying subscriber base.
insights.speaker: Dick Costolo
insights.so_what: A specific, actionable M&A idea: Snap's clip-distribution infrastructure could be more valuable to a content platform like Netflix than its current standalone valuation implies.
insights.quote: If I was Netflix, I'd buy Snap like this.

insights.claim: Costolo and Nathan agree Tesla's core EV business has been badly damaged after Musk started a price war in late 2022/early 2023 that misjudged price elasticity, causing significant share loss, and argue SpaceX/Tesla shareholders would be better served by capital going toward Optimus and the robotaxi (Cybercab) business rather than the legacy EV business or any Tesla-SpaceX merger.
insights.speaker: Dick Costolo
insights.so_what: A bearish read on Tesla's core auto business fundamentals, paired with a view that capital reallocation toward robotics/robotaxi is the more investable thesis within the Musk complex.
insights.quote: the EV business is dead. It's over.

themes.theme: Physical AI and robotics as the next investment wave

insights.claim: Costolo expects defense and industrial applications to be the first wave of humanoid-robot adoption (already underway), while general-purpose humanoid robots in the home remain further out due to safety and liability concerns.
insights.speaker: Dick Costolo
insights.so_what: Suggests investors should weight near-term robotics exposure toward defense/industrial suppliers and integrators rather than consumer-home robotics plays.

insights.claim: Costolo says humanoid-robot capability is likely to improve faster than expected, drawing an analogy to how Anthropic and OpenAI's models went from 'cute' to 'really really good' surprisingly quickly, and 01 Advisors is now evaluating an enablement-layer investment thesis for robotics analogous to its AI enablement-layer thesis.
insights.speaker: Dick Costolo
insights.so_what: Positions robotics/physical AI enablement software as a forward-looking extension of 01 Advisors' current AI infrastructure thesis, worth watching for early deal announcements.

insights.claim: Costolo says roughly 90% of prediction-market participants (on platforms like Kalshi) lose money or fail to profit, yet in his experience most users describe themselves as doing well -- a stark gap between self-reported performance and actual outcomes.
insights.speaker: Dick Costolo
insights.so_what: A behavioral-finance red flag for the fast-growing prediction-market category: reported user sentiment/engagement metrics may materially overstate actual participant profitability.
insights.quote: 90% of people lose money or don't make money on prediction markets.
